summary:
We created a health monitoring software MindOrbit that integrates physical measurements, journaling and cognitive indicators. It detects subtle changes in behaviour and physical health from data uploaded by the astronaut while ensuring that privacy is kept through the various controls. The data obtained from the astronaut's inputs will help the LLM provide astronauts with the ability to assess their physical and psychological health, understand how spaceflight affects their wellbeing, and receive actionable guidance to maintain or improve their health.
As astronauts are high achieving individuals, they are more likely to be private about matters regarding their health that could compromise their image which can affect their candidacy for the role. This helps to give them an avenue to feel safe while sharing their information. Furthermore, astronauts are only human and they will therefore be susceptible physical and psychological health issues of varying severity. With the wide and comprehensive functions of our project, it helps to provide an all-encompassing method to ensure that any issue is detected and dealt with early.
details:
MindOrbit — Beyond Monitoring, Towards Meaningful Intervention

MindOrbit is a privacy-first, AI-powered astronaut health companion designed to help astronauts independently assess and manage their physical, cognitive, and psychological wellbeing during long-duration space missions.

What does MindOrbit do, and how does it work?

Spaceflight exposes astronauts to unique health challenges, including microgravity, isolation, disrupted sleep, demanding workloads, and limited access to immediate medical assistance. MindOrbit addresses these challenges by integrating health monitoring, personalised analysis, AI-assisted explanations, and guided interventions into a single interactive platform.

The software allows astronauts to manually record or import time-stamped health measurements, including heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), blood pressure, sleep duration, and cognitive performance. Instead of relying solely on generic thresholds, MindOrbit calculates individual baselines using historical measurements and identifies potentially meaningful deviations. Its interactive dashboard displays health trends, relevant contextual factors, and explanations of why particular changes may deserve attention.

MindOrbit also incorporates private psychological journaling. With explicit user consent, the software locally analyses linguistic characteristics such as lexical diversity, word count, and sentence length. By comparing writing patterns over time, it can highlight changes that may warrant further reflection without treating them as definitive indicators of psychological disorders.

At the centre of MindOrbit is Orbit, an AI companion powered by Gemma 3 4B through Ollama. Operating locally, Orbit helps astronauts understand their health measurements, explore possible contributing factors, and receive contextual guidance without depending on cloud-based AI services.

A separate rule-based decision engine determines which support resources are appropriate for the identified concerns. These include breathing exercises, grounding techniques, sleep guidance, social connection activities, and workload reflection. The AI explains these options but cannot independently override safety rules or generate unrestricted medical treatments.

A key feature is MindOrbit's intervention effectiveness tracking. Astronauts can select a recommended activity, record their participation, and review subsequent health measurements. The system compares measurements before and after the activity to identify improvements or continuing concerns, while acknowledging that observed changes do not necessarily establish causation.

What are the benefits and intended impact?

MindOrbit aims to transform astronaut health monitoring from passive data collection into proactive, understandable, and actionable health support.

By combining physiological measurements with psychological and cognitive information, the software provides a more comprehensive picture of astronaut wellbeing. Personalised baselines account for individual differences, while contextual explanations help prevent misleading interpretations of isolated measurements.

Its offline-first architecture is particularly relevant to deep-space missions, where communication delays can limit immediate access to Earth-based specialists. MindOrbit allows astronauts to continue reviewing health information and accessing supportive resources locally.

Privacy is another central benefit. Personal measurements, journal entries, and intervention records are stored in an encrypted local browser database when secure storage is available. Raw journals are excluded from automatic AI analysis, and users must explicitly approve sharing derived linguistic summaries with Orbit.

Ultimately, MindOrbit aims to encourage earlier recognition of health concerns, support informed self-assessment, and improve access to appropriate wellbeing resources. Its underlying approach could also benefit people working in isolated or remote environments on Earth.

What technologies did we use?

MindOrbit was developed using JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and Node.js to create a responsive web application with interactive dashboards, health visualisations, and user-controlled data entry.

We integrated Google's Gemma 3 4B large language model, operated locally through Ollama, to provide conversational support and explainable health feedback without requiring cloud inference.

Custom JavaScript algorithms perform time-series analysis, calculate personalised health baselines, extract linguistic features from journals, and evaluate changes following interventions. A separate deterministic decision engine manages monitoring rules and permitted support recommendations.

For data protection, MindOrbit uses IndexedDB with AES-GCM encryption for local storage. A service worker enables offline access to cached application features and support resources.

The prototype runs on an ordinary computer without specialised hardware. Health measurements can be entered manually or imported, while fictional astronaut datasets are used to demonstrate monitoring and intervention workflows. No physical medical sensors are currently connected.

How is MindOrbit creative?

MindOrbit's innovation lies in connecting health assessment, explainable AI, personalised intervention, and outcome evaluation within one astronaut-centred system.

Unlike conventional monitoring dashboards that primarily display measurements or flag abnormalities, MindOrbit helps astronauts understand what has changed, consider possible explanations, explore appropriate support options, and evaluate subsequent progress.

Its personalised monitoring approach also extends to psychological journaling, using changes in measurable writing patterns rather than relying exclusively on negative keywords or generic sentiment analysis.

Most importantly, MindOrbit introduces a continuous feedback process:

Detect → Explain → Support → Evaluate → Follow up.

This shifts the focus from simply identifying potential problems to helping astronauts respond meaningfully to them.

What factors did our team consider?

Our team prioritised privacy, reliability, individual differences, explainability, and practical feasibility.

We recognised that astronauts may hesitate to disclose psychological concerns if they fear unnecessary exposure of sensitive information. Consequently, MindOrbit uses local AI processing, encrypted storage, optional journal analysis, and explicit consent controls.

We also considered the limitations of AI interpretation. Changes in language, heart rate, or sleep patterns can arise from many causes, including exercise, workload, illness, and normal individual variation. MindOrbit therefore incorporates contextual information, displays uncertainty, and avoids automatically diagnosing medical or psychiatric conditions.

To reduce inappropriate recommendations, the system separates deterministic monitoring and safety rules from the language model's conversational functions. It also provides clearly labelled fallback guidance when local AI inference is unavailable.

Finally, we designed the prototype to be accessible and feasible without specialised hardware, using simulated mission scenarios to demonstrate its capabilities.

MindOrbit remains a proof-of-concept rather than a clinically validated medical system. Future development would require validated medical thresholds, professional oversight, sensor integration, and extensive testing before operational deployment.

MindOrbit represents our vision of astronaut healthcare that goes beyond monitoring—helping astronauts understand their health, take informed action, and remain supported even when Earth is far away.
